                                      PROJECT NO. 58481

 RULEMAKING TO ESTABLISH                          §   PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                       §
 STANDARDS UNDER PURA 37.0561                     §               OF TEXAS



             ROWAN DIGITAL INFRASTRUCTURE LLC REPLY COMMENTS

         Rowan Digital Infrastructure LLC (“Rowan”), acting on its own behalf and on behalf of its
project-level subsidiaries that are developing data centers in ERCOT, welcomes the opportunity
to provide feedback in response to the Public Utility Commission of Texas (“Commission”) Staff
discussion draft of the new 16 Texas Administrative Code (“TAC”) § 25.194 implementing Senate
Bill 6 (“SB 6”) and Public Utility Regulatory Act (“PURA”) § 37.0561 large load interconnection
standards (the “Discussion Draft”). Rowan works with local electric and water utilities, retail
electricity providers (“REPs”), and other energy partners to develop, own, and operate build-to-
suit and turnkey hyperscale data centers for some of the largest technology companies in the world.
At present, Rowan has multiple hyperscale data center sites under development in Texas, including
in Lytle and Temple. Rowan appreciates the opportunity to provide its perspective on the
Discussion Draft and related questions. Rowan respectfully submits the following comments.
Rowan looks forward to participating further in the large load rulemaking process both at the
Commission and at ERCOT, and reserves the ability to submit additional or revised comments as
this process moves forward.
                                      I.     INTRODUCTION
    Rowan supports the Commission’s general approach in this Discussion Draft. Rowan offers
the below comments to provide additional context and perspective from its experience as an entity
that develops, owns, and operates large data centers through long-term leases with tenants. Rowan
provides these recommendations to tailor the Commission’s Discussion Draft to satisfy the
requirements and policies of SB 6 without unduly burdening the commercial large load
development process.
                       II.   ROWAN RESPONSE TO DISCUSSION QUESTIONS
    Rowan offers the following comments regarding the questions posed in the Discussion Draft:




HB: 4916-8367-6788.4
                                                                                             000001
     1. Discussion Question: Should the commission define parameters for determining
         whether a large load customer is pursuing a substantially similar interconnection
         request? If so, how should the commission define those parameters?
    No, the Commission should not define parameters for disclosing a substantially similar
interconnection request. Rowan cautions that the Commission should not create an overly
restrictive definition of “substantially similar interconnection request” that may inaccurately
presume that a large load customer will not continue to pursue multiple similar interconnection
requests if one is approved.
    As a developer, owner, and operator of data centers for technology companies, Rowan may
from time to time submit two or more large load requests that may on their face appear
substantially similar, but which are for entirely independent projects, each of which would proceed
regardless of whether approval of the other interconnection request is granted. Given the nature of
data center demand and development, these facially similar but distinct interconnection requests
may be for loads that are proximate to one another, share similar or overlapping capacity requests
and energization timelines, or involve the same end-use customers. Nevertheless, the approval of
one would not affect the other. If the Commission definition and rule on this point is too restrictive,
a large load customer may be required to disclose similar, but completely independent, projects,
thus introducing significant uncertainty for the interconnecting utility and regulators in interpreting
the information disclosed under this rule.
    Accordingly, rather than establish detailed parameters for what constitutes a “substantially
similar” interconnection request, Rowan recommends that the Commission require a large load
customer to submit an attestation to the interconnecting electric utility, in which the large load
customer indicates whether it is pursuing a substantially similar interconnection request in Texas,
the approval of which would result in the customer materially changing, delaying, or withdrawing
the interconnection request. This approach is directly aligned with SB 6’s requirements and
addresses policy concerns about duplicative interconnection requests without imposing arbitrary
or overly broad definitions that fail to capture the realities of project development.
    2. Discussion Question: Proposed subsections (c)(3), (e)(3), and (h)(3) require the
         disclosure of specific information related to a substantially similar request for
         interconnection and allows a large load customer to anonymize competitively
         sensitive details. Should the commission list what is and is not competitively sensitive



HB: 4916-8367-6788.4
                                                                                                 000002
          (e.g., load zone is not competitively sensitive information)? If so, what information
         should and should not be considered competitively sensitive such that the
         interconnecting utility and ERCOT can identify whether there is a duplicate request,
         or a request is unlikely to materialize?
    Rowan appreciates the need for the interconnecting utility and regulators to reduce the number
of duplicative or overly speculative load requests in the interconnection queue. However, at a
minimum, the Commission’s protections for competitively sensitive information under this section
should at minimum afford the same level of protection provided to a large load customer’s
information under the ERCOT Protocols. For example, under NPRR 1267, ERCOT is required to
maintain the confidentiality of large load customer data when publishing its monthly Large Load
Interconnection status report, including the following data:
    a) Load zone;
    b) The Transmission Service Provider (TSP);
    c) Load type (as provided to the TSP, such as a refinery, steel mill, data center, etc.);
    d) Calendar quarter and year in which the interconnecting TSP submitted the project to
         ERCOT;
    e) Requested energization quarter and year;
    f) Size range;
    g) Interconnection status (as defined by ERCOT to differentiate between operational,
         approved under study, etc.); and
    h) Co-location status.
    At minimum, Commission rules should allow a large load customer to anonymize the above
categories of information, consistent with NPRR 1267, which has been approved by the
Commission. The Commission should also allow a large load customer to anonymize information
that constitutes Protected Information as defined in ERCOT Protocols Section 1.3.1.1 or ERCOT
Critical Energy Infrastructure Information (ECEII) under Protocols Section 1.3.2.1.
    Additionally, Rowan encourages the Commission to protect information about the identity of
the end-use customer and dynamic modeling information because this information can be
exploited by a large load customer’s competitors and its commercial customers.
    3. Discussion Question: Should the commission require a large load customer to notify
         the interconnecting electric utility and ERCOT of any change to information that is



HB: 4916-8367-6788.4
                                                                                                000003
          initially disclosed in response to this rule or only material changes to the information
         disclosed? If only material changes, how should “material change” be defined?
    Rowan recommends that a large load customer should be required to disclose only a material
change to previously disclosed information, not other non-material changes not affecting the
matters under study. To provide clarity and certainty, a material change should be defined to only
include a significant change to the project’s location or MW size. This definition ensures that
regulators and the interconnecting electric utility are informed of material changes that may affect
load interconnection, while ensuring that the large load customer is not obligated to disclose minor
changes and the interconnecting electric utility and regulators are not burdened by frequent updates
on changes to minor project details.
    4. Discussion Question: Proposed subsection (k)(1) authorizes an interconnecting
         electric utility to refund 20% of a large load customer’s security after energization
         and ratably as the large load customer meets the milestones identified in the
         customer’s schedule for phased energization of its contracted load. Should the
         commission standardize the rate for refund for reaching milestones identified in the
         customer’s schedule for phased energization (e.g., 20% for each year of operations
         until the full amount of security is refunded)? If so, how should the commission
         standardize the refund?
    Yes, the Commission should standardize the rate for refund for reaching milestones in the
customer energization schedule to remove discrepancies and uncertainty between interconnecting
electric utilities. Rowan encourages the Commission to structure the standardized schedule and
rate of refund so that it aligns with interconnecting electric utility’s cost recovery timeline from
the load customer.
    5. Discussion Question: Are changes to the commission’s other substantive rules
         necessary to align with this rulemaking? If so, what changes need to be made to which
         rules?
    Rowan urges the Commission to ensure consistency in the definitions and standards across all
SB 6 rulemakings to prevent confusion and inconsistent application across interconnecting electric
utilities and large load customers. Rowan would encourage Staff and stakeholders to identify any
such inconsistencies or other rule provisions that merit modifications to meet this interest.




HB: 4916-8367-6788.4
                                                                                                000004
                        III.   ROWAN COMMENTS TO DISCUSSION DRAFT
         Rowan also provides comments and recommendations on the following Discussion Draft
    subsections:
    A. Definitions – 16 TAC 25.194(b)
    Consistent with its response to Questions 1 and 3, Rowan offers the following definitions:


(12) Competitively sensitive information — includes but is not limited to the following
information pertaining to a large load interconnection request:
         (a) Load zone;
         (b) Transmission service provider;
         (c) The load type;
         (d) The calendar quarter and year in which the interconnecting transmission service
         provider submitted the project to ERCOT;
         (e) The requested energization quarter and year;
         (f) The capacity or capacity range of the load;
         (g) The interconnection status;
         (h) The co-location status of the project;
         (i) Dynamic modeling information;
         (j) The identity of the end-use customer or ultimate parent entity;
         (k) Information that constitutes protected information or ERCOT critical energy
         infrastructure information pursuant to the ERCOT protocols; or
         (l) Any other information that, if disclosed, could reasonably be expected to provide a
         competitive advantage to another market participant or harm the applicant’s business
         interests.
(13) Material change — a change that:
         (a) constitutes a significant change to a project’s geographical location or capacity; or
         (b) would reasonably be expected to result in the withdrawal or cancellation of the
         interconnection request.


    B. Large Load Interconnection Study – 16 TAC 25.194(d)
    Consistent with its response to Question 3, Rowan offers the change below, which would revise
the draft 16 TAC 25.194(d)(1) to require a large load customer to disclose only a material change
to the interconnecting electric utility. Additionally, Rowan proposes that a large load customer
should have 30 days, rather than a mere five days, to disclose such a material change. The 30-day


HB: 4916-8367-6788.4
                                                                                                000005
 timeline is more consistent with the Commission’s other requirements regarding notice of a
material change. 1


                   (1) Within 30 5 days of a material change to the information disclosed under
                       subsection (c) of this section, the large load customer must notify the
                       interconnecting electric utility of this change.


    C. Discretionary Services Agreement – 16 TAC § 25.194(e)
              a. Financial Commitment
    Rowan supports the use of financial commitments at the discretionary services agreement
phase to cull speculative projects. However, Rowan believes the $50,000 per MW of contracted
peak demand prescribed in the draft 16 TAC § 25.194(e)(8) is too high of a financial commitment
for the discretionary services agreement phase, and may unnecessarily restrict large load
development. Instead, Rowan strongly recommends that the draft 16 TAC § 25.194(e)(8) financial
commitment be set at $10,000 per MW of contracted peak demand. Rowan believes this amount
achieves a better balance between reducing speculative requests while acknowledging the
commercial realities for developers at this phase of project development.
              b. Site-Related Studies, Engineering Services, and State and Local Regulatory
                   Approvals.
    Rowan believes the requirements under the draft 16 TAC § 25.194(e)(4)-(5) are too subjective
and vague. Rowan recognizes the interconnecting electric utility’s interest in confirming that a
large load customer is making necessary progress on project development. However, an
interconnecting electric utility is not well-positioned to independently evaluate these submissions.
Each large load development requires a unique set of site-related studies, engineering services, and
regulatory approvals. An interconnecting electric utility likely lacks the expertise and time to
verify these proposed disclosures and to adequately evaluate progress on each site-specific
development requirement. These requirements impose an unnecessary administrative burden on
the customer to provide information that provides little benefit to the interconnecting electric



1
 For example, a Power Generation Company has 30 days to amend its registration and notify the Commission of a
change to certain contact information or a change in its corporate parent company. See 16 Texas Administrative
Code § 25.109(f)(1), (3).


HB: 4916-8367-6788.4
                                                                                                         000006
 utility. These requirements would also impose an unnecessary administrative burden on the electric
utility to evaluate matters that are outside its usual scope of expertise. Accordingly, Rowan
recommends that the Commission remove the requirements in draft 16 TAC § 25.194(e)(4)-(5), as
shown below:


                   (4)   Site-related studies and engineering services. A large load customer must
                         submit to the interconnecting electric utility the large load customer’s plans,
                         expected timing, and progress for site-related studies and engineering
                         services required for project development before energization (e.g., water,
                         wastewater, or gas). The submission must be accompanied by an attestation
                         by an officer or official with binding authority over the large load customer
                         stating that the information contained in the submission is complete and
                         accurate at the time the attestation is signed. A large load customer must
                         provide updates or progress reports to the interconnecting electric utility
                         when requested.
                   (5)   State and local regulatory approvals. A large load customer must submit
                         to the interconnecting electric utility describing the large load customer’s
                         plans, expected timing, and current progress for obtaining state and local
                         regulatory approvals required for development before energization (e.g.,
                         water, air, or backup generation permits, or city or county building permits).
                         The submission must be accompanied by an attestation by an officer or
                         official with binding authority over the large load customer attesting that
                         the information contained in the submission is complete and accurate at the
                         time the attestation is signed. A large load customer must provide updates
                         or progress reports to the interconnecting electric utility when requested.


    D. Intermediate Agreement - 16 TAC § 25.194(h)
              a. Site Control
    Rowan recommends that at the intermediate agreement stage in draft 16 TAC § 25.194(h)(2),
the Commission should still recognize an option to lease or purchase as a valid method of site
control, rather than only permit an executed lease or deed to serve as a sufficient demonstration of



HB: 4916-8367-6788.4
                                                                                                  000007
 site control. For a data center developer at this intermediate phase of development, there is still
considerable optionality in determining what constitutes commercially necessary and reasonable
site control. A developer often obtains an option to purchase or lease more land than will eventually
be required for the data center facility. Prior to interconnection agreement execution, the method
of site control is generally finalized and an option to purchase or lease may be executed for the
portions of the property necessary for the site. A premature requirement to lease or acquire by deed
all property potentially necessary at this intermediate agreement stage is not commercially
reasonable and will unnecessarily tie up land that will not be required for the data center facility.
These practices occur not just with data centers, but with generation facilities under development
and in the interconnection queue as well, and both ERCOT and transmission and/or distribution
service providers (TDSPs) will be well familiar with the practice that developers firm up site
control as the project moves through development and financing steps. The rule here should not
impose a higher burden in this specific instance than generally applies in other similar
interconnection circumstances.
    Instead, Rowan urges the Commission to recognize a legally binding option to purchase or
lease as sufficient site control in the intermediate agreement. A legally binding option to purchase
or lease, paired with the other reasonable requirements in this subsection, demonstrates sufficient
readiness and legitimacy. Allowing an option to purchase or lease at this stage also prevents
unnecessary and wasteful acquisition of land at this phase of development.
              b. Site-Related Studies, Engineering Services, and State and Local Regulatory
                   Approvals.
    As urged above regarding draft 16 TAC § 25.194(e)(4)-(5), relating to discretionary service
agreement requirements, Rowan reiterates the same points regarding the intermediate agreement
requirements under 16 TAC § 25.194(h)(4)-(5). These requirements regarding site-related studies,
engineering services, and state and local regulatory approvals are vague, subjective, and
unnecessary. Accordingly, Rowan recommends the Commission remove the requirements in 16
TAC § 25.194(h)(4)-(5), as shown below:


                   (1)   Site-related studies and engineering services. A large load customer must
                         submit to the interconnecting electric utility the large load customer’s plans,
                         expected timing, and progress for site-related studies and engineering



HB: 4916-8367-6788.4
                                                                                                  000008
                          services required for project development before energization (e.g., water,
                         wastewater, or gas). The submission must be accompanied by an attestation
                         by an officer or official with binding authority over the large load customer
                         stating that the information contained in the submission is complete and
                         accurate at the time the attestation is signed. A large load customer must
                         provide updates or progress reports to the interconnecting electric utility
                         when requested.
                   (2)   State and local regulatory approvals. A large load customer must submit
                         to the interconnecting electric utility describing the large load customer’s
                         plans, expected timing, and current progress for obtaining state and local
                         regulatory approvals required for development before energization (e.g.,
                         water, air, or backup generation permits, or city or county building permits).
                         The submission must be accompanied by an attestation by an officer or
                         official with binding authority over the large load customer attesting that
                         the information contained in the submission is complete and accurate at the
                         time the attestation is signed. A large load customer must provide updates
                         or progress reports to the interconnecting electric utility when requested.



Dated December 19, 2025




                                                Respectfully submitted,



                                                ROWAN DIGITAL INFRASTRUCTURE LLC

                                          EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

    •    Discussion Question 1: Instead of defining parameters for what constitutes a “substantially
         similar” interconnection request, the Commission should adopt an attestation requirement whereby,
         if applicable, a large load customer must submit an attestation to the interconnecting electric utility
         in which the large load customer indicates that it is pursuing a substantially similar interconnection
         request in Texas, the approval of which would result in the customer materially changing, delaying,
         or withdrawing the interconnection request.
    •    Discussion Question 2: The protections for competitively sensitive information under this rule
         should accord with the protections provided for a large load customer’s information under the
         ERCOT Protocols, including information that may be anonymized under NPRR 1267 and
         information that constitutes Protected Information or ECEII under the Protocols.
    •    Discussion Question 3: A large load customer should only be required to provide an update
         regarding a material change, expressly limited to a change to project location or capacity.
    •    Discussion Question 4: The Commission should standardize the rate for refund for reaching
         milestones in the customer energization schedule and align it with the utility’s cost recovery
         timeline from the load.
    •    Discussion Question 5: The Commission should ensure consistency in definitions and standards
         across all SB 6 rulemakings.
    •    16 TAC § 25.194(e) - Discretionary Services Agreement Financial Commitment: The
         $50,000 per MW financial commitment is too onerous; the financial commitment at this phase
         should be $10,000 per MW.
    •    16 TAC § 25.194(e) - Discretionary Services Agreement: The site-related studies, engineering
         services, and state and local approvals requirements under this section are too subjective and
         vague and should be deleted.
    •    16 TAC § 25.194(h) - Intermediate Agreement Site Control: The Commission should accept a
         legally binding option to purchase or lease as sufficient demonstration of site control at the
         intermediate agreement phase.
    •    16 TAC § 25.194(h) - Intermediate Agreement: The site-related studies, engineering services,
         and non-electric state and local regulatory approvals requirements under this section should be
         removed, as evaluation of such matters falls outside the expertise of the interconnecting utility.

              a. Financial Commitment
    Rowan supports the use of financial commitments at the discretionary services agreement
phase to cull speculative projects. However, Rowan believes the $50,000 per MW of contracted
peak demand prescribed in the draft 16 TAC § 25.194(e)(8) is too high of a financial commitment
for the discretionary services agreement phase, and may unnecessarily restrict large load
development. Instead, Rowan strongly recommends that the draft 16 TAC § 25.194(e)(8) financial
commitment be set at $10,000 per MW of contracted peak demand. Rowan believes this amount
achieves a better balance between reducing speculative requests while acknowledging the
commercial realities for developers at this phase of project development.
              b. Site-Related Studies, Engineering Services, and State and Local Regulatory
                   Approvals.
    Rowan believes the requirements under the draft 16 TAC § 25.194(e)(4)-(5) are too subj ective
and vague. Rowan recognizes the interconnecting electric utility' s interest in confirming that a
large load customer is making necessary progress on project development. However, an
interconnecting electric utility is not well-positioned to independently evaluate these submissions.
Each large load development requires a unique set of site-related studies, engineering services, and
regulatory approvals. An interconnecting electric utility likely lacks the expertise and time to
verify these proposed disclosures and to adequately evaluate progress on each site-specific
development requirement. These requirements impose an unnecessary administrative burden on
the customer to provide information that provides little benefit to the interconnecting electric

    D. Intermediate Agreement - 16 TAC § 25.194(h)
              a. Site Control
    Rowan recommends that at the intermediate agreement stage in draft 16 TAC § 25.194(h)(2),
the Commission should still recognize an option to lease or purchase as a valid method of site
control, rather than only permit an executed lease or deed to serve as a sufficient demonstration of

 site control. For a data center developer at this intermediate phase of development, there is still
considerable optionality in determining what constitutes commercially necessary and reasonable
site control. A developer often obtains an option to purchase or lease more land than will eventually
be required for the data center facility. Prior to interconnection agreement execution, the method
of site control is generally finalized and an option to purchase or lease may be executed for the
portions ofthe property necessary for the site. A premature requirement to lease or acquire by deed
all property potentially necessary at this intermediate agreement stage is not commercially
reasonable and will unnecessarily tie up land that will not be required for the data center facility.
These practices occur not just with data centers, but with generation facilities under development
and in the interconnection queue as well, and both ERCOT and transmission and/or distribution
service providers (TDSPs) will be well familiar with the practice that developers firm up site
control as the project moves through development and financing steps. The rule here should not
impose a higher burden in this specific instance than generally applies in other similar
interconnection circumstances.
    Instead, Rowan urges the Commission to recognize a legally binding option to purchase or
lease as sufficient site control in the intermediate agreement. A legally binding option to purchase
or lease, paired with the other reasonable requirements in this subsection, demonstrates sufficient
readiness and legitimacy. Allowing an option to purchase or lease at this stage also prevents
unnecessary and wasteful acquisition of land at this phase of development.

                                          EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

    •    Discussion Question 1: Instead of defining parameters for what constitutes a "substantially
         similar" interconnection request, the Commission should adopt an attestation requirement whereby,
         if applicable, a large load customer must submit an attestation to the interconnecting electric utility
         in which the large load customer indicates that it is pursuing a substantially similar interconnection
         request in Texas, the approval of which would result in the customer materially changing, delaying,
         or withdrawing the interconnection request.
    •    Discussion Question 2: The protections for competitively sensitive information under this rule
         should accord with the protections provided for a large load customer's information under the
         ERCOT Protocols, including information that may be anonymized under NPRR 1267 and
         information that constitutes Protected Information or ECEII under the Protocols.
    •    Discussion Question 3: A large load customer should only be required to provide an update
         regarding a material change, expressly limited to a change to project location or capacity.
    •    Discussion Question 4: The Commission should standardize the rate for refund for reaching
         milestones in the customer energization schedule and align it with the utility's cost recovery
         timeline from the load.
    •    Discussion Question 5: The Commission should ensure consistency in definitions and standards
         across all SB 6 rulemakings.
    •    16 TAC § 25.194(e) - Discretionary Services Agreement Financial Commitment: The
         $50,000 per MW financial commitment is too onerous; the financial commitment at this phase
         should be $10,000 per MW.

         services, and state and local approvals requirements under this section are too subjective and
